RAKOW, J:
Introduction
[1]	The plaintiff is Fillipus Aiaseb, an adult male Namibian person and currently a serving inmate at the Windhoek Correctional Facility with prison number ON-1-18917.  The first defendant is the minister of Home Affairs, Immigration, Safety and Security in his duly appointed and official capacity in terms of Article 32(3)(i)(bb) of the Constitution of the Republic of Namibian.  The second defendant is the Commissioner-General of the Namibian Correctional Service in his duly appointed and official capacity in terms of article 34(4)(c)(cc) of the Constitution of the Republic of Namibia.  The third defendant is S.S. Shanghala, a correctional officer at the Windhoek Correctional Facility.

Cause of action and plea

[2]	It is alleged that the cause of action arose on 2 May 2022 at around 17h30 when the plaintiff was unlawfully and intentionally physically assaulted by the third defendant and plus minus 15 other unknown correctional officers in his prison cell at the Windhoek Correctional Facility for allegedly aiding an inmate to escape the said facility.  It is alleged that he was kicked with booted feet and slapped all over his body and head.  This assault then continued after he was handcuffed and taken to the dining hall of Unit 4.

[3]	As a result of these assaults, the plaintiff suffered a fractured and broken central incisor; swollen and bleeding gums; chest pains; swollen head and body; wrist pains and superficial injuries and a swollen and sub-conjunctival hemorrhage left eye.  As a result of this assault, the plaintiff further suffered contumelia.  The plaintiff therefore claimed damages in the amount of N$1 500 000 as a result of the physical assault, N$500 00 for contumelia and a further N$500 000 for future medical expenses.  

[4]	The defendants pleaded that on or about 2 May 2022 the defendants and/or correctional officers employed by the first defendant, including the third defendant were investigating a matter of escape from lawful custody by an inmate known as Simon Kambindu at Unit 4.  During this investigation they were lead to the plaintiff and they were informed that the plaintiff was in possession of a cell phone which is prohibited in the facility.  It was believed that the plaintiff used this cell phone to communicate with the escapee prior to his escape from lawful custody.  	

[5]	They proceeded to question the plaintiff as to whether he was indeed in possession of such a cell phone and he denied it.  He further became aggressive, violent and refused and resisted to be searched.  Due to this, the third defendant instructed the plaintiff to be handcuffed and he was informed the handcuffs would only be removed once he cooperates and hand over the cell phone.  The plaintiff was never physically assaulted by the third defendant or 15 other correctional officers.

The evidence
The plaintiff

[6]	The plaintiff testified that on 2 May 2022 at 17h30, when it was lock up time, he was in his cell in the bathroom busy washing his clothes.  He heard that all the other inmates were informed to leave the cell except him.  He was approached by the third defendant and told that he helped a fellow inmate to escape the facility and that he was in possession of a cell phone.  He denied that and was slapped with an open hand on the face.  After this slap, the other officers joined in and also assaulted him.  Due to the assault he fell on the floor and then some officers stomped on his head, which in turn caused his head to hit the floor where he broke his tooth.  They then proceeded to cuff him in the number 8 position and took him to the dining hall.  At that stage his mouth was bleeding.  

[7]	At the dining hall the third defendant assaulted him again and he was informed that the escapee was found with a phone with a contact “Dix” and when confronted, he informed the officers that it is the plaintiff.  The plaintiff then informed the officers that he received a phone from Richard Katjatenja but that the phone was returned to him.  They then proceeded to collect the phone from Richard Katjatenja.  The Senior Superintendent Sakaria informed the officers to take the plaintiff to the clinic where he received pain medication and the next day he was taken to hospital where they removed the remainder of his tooth.

[8]	During cross-examination the plaintiff was confronted with the fact that the medical report indicated that the tooth broke horizontally.  He further indicated that his wrists were tender, his chest and his stomach pained, he had a red spot in his eye and his knees were also sore.  

Linus Nzwana 

[9]	The witness is an adult male currently incarcerated at the Windhoek Correctional Facility.  On 2 May 2022 at lock-up time he was in a cell.  He saw officers passing by the windows and the inmates were ordered not to move.  The cell was opened and some officers went into the cell whilst others went into the bathroom.  The inmates in the cell were told to leave the cell after they were searched.  The plaintiff and a certain Ian Jones were left in the cell.  He heard the plaintiff scream.  After some time he was brought out, handcuffed in a nr.8 position.  The witness saw blood on his mouth and his t-shirt and he heard the plaintiff telling the officers that they broke his tooth.  When the plaintiff returned, he complained the whole time and he took pain medication.  He also saw the plaintiff with a swollen lip.

Linus Hindjou

[10]	Mr Hindjou testified that he is an adult male person, currently incarcerated at the Windhoek Correctional Facility.  At about 17h00 on 2 May 2022, the officers came looking for the plaintiff who was also an inmate and sharing the cell with the witness.  The plaintiff and a certain Ian Jones were in the toilet at that time and the plaintiff was washing his clothes.  The inmates were ordered to leave the cell and waited outside.  He heard the plaintiff crying out :  “Julle maak my seer” which means that he was being hurt and he also heard banging sounds.  Afterwards the officers took out the plaintiff and he was handcuffed in the nr.8 position.  He had blood on his mouth and his t-shirt.  When they returned to the cell he noted that the bed of the plaintiff was moved and there were blood stains on the floor.  He also heard the plaintiff complain of having pain that night.

Ian Jones

[11]	The witness is an adult male and also incarcerated at the Windhoek Correctional Facility.  On 2 May 2022 he was playing cards in front of the bathroom when he saw officers pass the window.  He went into the toilet to disconnect the stove.  He found the plaintiff in the toilet busy washing his clothes.  They were ordered to stand still and he and the plaintiff were handcuffed.  The next moment he saw the plaintiff on the floor and he saw a correctional service member from unit 4 stomping on the plaintiff’s head with his booted feet.  He heard the head of the plaintiff hit the floor.  He was then taken out of the toilet to the left side of the cell and his cupboard was searched.  In order to reach his cupboard he had to pass the door to the toilet.  When he passed the door, he saw some officers kicking and beating the plaintiff who was still on the floor.  There after he was taken outside and then observed the plaintiff being taken from the cell.  He had blood on his mouth and was in pain.  When the plaintiff returned to the cell at a later stage, he saw that the tooth of the plaintiff was indeed broken.  

Defense

Sakaria Ipinge

[12]	The witness is a major male, employed at the Windhoek Correctional Facility as a Senior Superintendent and the Head of Security at the facility.  On 1 May 2022 an offender, Simon Kambindu escaped from custody at the Windhoek Correctional Facility.  When they learned of the escape, he ordered a search of units 4 and 6.  They retrieved a cell phone from a certain Stefanus Mwandingi which indicated that the person was in contact with the escapee as well as a certain “Dix” who was later identified by Stefanus Mwandingi as the plaintiff.  The witness then instructed the other correctional officers to carry out a search in unit 6 where the plaintiff was housed.

[13]	The witness initially remained in the dining hall of unit 4 but later followed the other officers to unit 6.   When he came there, he found the plaintiff handcuffed and being very aggressive.  Some officers managed to put him down on the floor and proceeded to handcuff him but not in a nr.8 position.  He was not assaulted or injured during this process. In terms of the Correctional Services Act 9 of 2012 and its regulations, officers are allowed to conduct searches and use minimal force when the circumstances require it.  After the plaintiff was handcuffed, the officers proceeded with him to the unit 4 dining hall. Here Stefanus Mwandingi indicated that he was indeed in contact with the plaintiff.  The plaintiff then informed the witness that he was using the phone of a certain Richard Katjitenga in unit 5.  He further informed the witness that he was in pain and the witness gave instructions that the plaintiff was to be taken to the clinic.  The plaintiff was at no time assaulted or kicked in the presence of the witness.

Tomas Shaanika

[14]	Tomas Shaanika holds the rank of Senior Chief Correctional Supervisor stationed at the Windhoek Correctional Facility and is also the Officer in Charge in unit 6 in the said facility.  On 2 May 2022 at about 16h00 a cell and body search was conducted at unit 4 and unit 6 of the facility.  The search was conducted in terms of s 38(1) of the Correctional Service Act, 9 of 2012 which allows a correctional officer to conduct a search of any offender who is within the correctional facility in the prescribed manner and circumstances.

[15]	Upon arrival at unit 6, the witness had the master key that opened all the gates of the cells in that unit.  He saw the plaintiff coming from the side of the bed section going to the bathroom.  He instructed all the offenders to stand next to their beds and informed them that a search would be conducted but the plaintiff remained in the bathroom.  After the offenders were searched, the witness instructed them to move outside the cell.  Ian Jones was also outside the cell and not inside the cell as he alluded in his testimony.  The witness was not inside the bathroom when the plaintiff was handcuffed and can therefore not say what happened there.  He however did not observe any injuries or blood on the plaintiff when he came outside the cell.  He was further not present when the plaintiff was taken to the dining hall.  He saw that the plaintiff was cuffed normally with his hands behind his back.

[16]	He further testified that the plaintiff used to complain to him to be taken to the hospital but he does not know the nature of the illness the plaintiff had.

Josef Moses

[17]	The witness is an Enrolled Nurse, employed by the Ministry of Home Affairs, Immigration, Safety and Security, and stationed at the Windhoek Correctional Facility.  On 2 May 2022 at about 17h45 he was at home on standby duty when he was called to the facility to see a patient, the plaintiff.  Upon his arrival at the clinic he found some officers who informed him that the plaintiff injured himself on the floor.  He proceeded and performed a physical examination on him.  He examined the plaintiff.  He further observed that the plaintiff had a history of a broken tooth, which he believes to be from an old injury.  He further proceeded to ask the plaintiff what his complaints were and the plaintiff indicated that he had injured himself on the floor.  He did not tell the witness how and what happened.  

[18]	According to the witness’ observation the plaintiff’s front tooth (number 11) had a loose part which was cracked from the inside, this is called an inner tooth fracture.  He observed that only the fractured part of the tooth was loose and the rest of the tooth was still intact.  He further indicated that in his expertise there should have been some bleeding in the mouth and some swelling if the fracture was recent and occurred on 2 May 2022.  He did however not observe any indication that suggested that the plaintiff fractured his tooth that day.  If he further injured himself on the floor, in the experience of the witness, he would have experienced an outer tooth fracture as opposed to an inner tooth fracture.

[19]	The plaintiff informed him that he was in pain and he administered a pain injection.  He also referred him to the dental clinic at the Katutura Hospital.  He was taken to the Katutura Hospital on 3 May 2022 where after he opted to see a private dental practitioner for further management.

Simeon Shangala

[20]	The third defendant is employed by the Ministry of Home Affairs, Immigration, Safety and Security:  Office of the Commissioner-General and holds the rank of Senior Chief Correctional Officer.  He is stationed at unit 3 at the Windhoek Correctional Facility.  On Monday, 2 May 2022 at 16h00, a cell and body search was conducted at unit 4 and 6 of the Windhoek Correctional Facility.  This was upon instructions from the Head of Security due to the unlawful escape from custody by an inmate Simon Kambindu.  During their search they found inmate Simon Kambundi with an illegal cell phone.  The call log indicated communication with a certain “Dix” whom was identified by the said Simon Kambindu at the plaintiff.  	

[21]	They proceeded to unit 6 and the witness saw the plaintiff moving from the bed section to the bathroom.  All the offenders were instructed to stand next to their beds and informed of the search.  The Plaintiff however remained in the bathroom but he was not washing his clothes as he testified.  The officers conducted a body search on the offenders and a sim card was found on the plaintiff.  The offenders were then instructed to stand outside the cell against the wall.  Only the plaintiff and the officers remained in the cell.  Ian Jones was not inside the cell.  The witness denies slapping the plaintiff with an open hand, neither that he kicked him in the stomach or head with booted feet.  When they found the sim card on him, they wanted to handcuff him and take him for further questioning.  The plaintiff however resisted and informed them that “whoever touches my body will see, I am having a lawyer”.  The officers then used minimal force to force the plaintiff to the ground and placed handcuffs on him.  He was not handcuffed in the nr.8 position.

[22]	The plaintiff did not break his tooth during this process, neither was he bleeding or had a swollen mouth and neither was he assaulted.  After he was handcuffed, the plaintiff was taken to the dining hall of unit 4 where Stefanus Mwandingi confirmed that he was communicating with the plaintiff on a cell phone.  The plaintiff then requested to speak to Senior Superintendent Sakaria where he informed him that the cell phone he used was with Richard Katjitenja.  

Exhibits
[23]	During the trial, the following documentary evidence was tendered:
(a) “Exhibit A” - Medical records of Katutura hospital and Oyetweni Dental Practice.
(b) “Exhibit B” - Affidavit in terms of s 212 (4) (a) of the Criminal Procedure Act 51 of 1977 (J88 report) 
(c) “Exhibit C” – Plaintiff’s health passport

Arguments by the parties

[24]	The Plaintiff’s version before the court was that he was assaulted by the correctional officers, slapped by the third Defendant (witness number 4), kicked with booted feet, and stomped on his head and in the process broke his tooth. Plaintiff further testified he was bleeding and his mouth was swollen, his version was corroborated by the three witnesses who came across as credible witnesses. The Defendant’s evidence is that the officers never assaulted the Plaintiff, they testified that minimum force as provided for by the Correctional Service Act and its Regulations was used to restrain and handcuff the Plaintiff as he was aggressive. All witnesses failed to put on record how the Plaintiff was aggressive. The Defendant’s further evidence was that the Plaintiff was restrained by approximately 8 officers. It was also the Defendant’s evidence that the Plaintiff was taken to the facility clinic after complaining of pain. The court is faced with two mutually destructive versions.

[25]	It was submitted that the explanation by the plaintiff that he broke this tooth that day, and he was bleeding and swollen, is the most probable version before the court. This version was corroborated by three witnesses, and the evidence that the plaintiff was bleeding and swollen was never refuted or challenged by the defendants legal practitioner during cross-examination. The evidence adduced by the plaintiff and his witnesses regarding the bleeding was left unchallenged in cross-examination.

[26]	It was further argued that the plaintiff testified that he was handcuffed and attacked by approximately 10 officers. This version was confirmed by the defendants witnesses that about 8 officers who were present. The defendants case was that they needed to use so many officers, because the plaintiff was aggressive; however, when put to the witnesses how aggressive the plaintiff was, they failed to demonstrate to the court. Witness Ipinge Sakaria was very evasive when the question of aggression was put to him, and as such, his evidence must be approached with caution. The only reasonable inference that can be drawn is that in this scuffle, comparing the ratio of the officers to the offender, the plaintiff lost his tooth in the process. The version that reflects what truly transpired on 2 May 2022 is that of the plaintiff.

[27]	It was argued on behalf of the defendants that it is a fact that in cases of assault, the plaintiff bears the onus to prove that there was a violation of his body by the defendants and that violation, if proved, I wrongful and unlawful. Once that is proved, the onus shifts to the defendants to find some sort of legal justification, such as self-defence.  In the current instance, this was not done and the only evidence before court suggests that the third defendant and fellow officers only used minimum force, as allowed for by legislation and regulations, to restrain the plaintiff and to subsequently cuff him.  There is no evidence that he was kicked with booted feet all over his body and head.

[28]	The plaintiff, during his evidence did not focus on any emotional and psychological shock, his claim is thus not substantiated. Rather, the plaintiff focused on the alleged assault and past and future medical expenses.

The legal considerations

[29]	In Harold Schmidt t/a Prestige Home Innovations v Heita it was held that: 

	‘The correct approach would be for the court to apply its mind not only to the merits and demerits of the two mutually destructive versions but also their probabilities and it is only after so applying its mind that the court would be justified in reaching the conclusion as to which opinion to accept and which to reject’

[30]	The court in the case of Von Wielligh v Shaumbwako adopted the reasoning when faced with disparate versions, as follows: 

	‘The plaintiff can only succeed if he satisfies the court on a preponderance of probabilities that his version is true and accurate and therefore acceptable, and that the other version advanced by the defendant is therefore false or mistaken and falls to be rejected. In deciding whether that evidence is true or not the Court will weigh up and test the plaintiff’s allegations against the general probabilities. The estimate of the credibility of a witness will therefore be inextricably bound up with the consideration of the probabilities of the case and, if the balance of probabilities favour the plaintiff then the Court will accept his version as being probably true.’

[31]	The principle of mutually destructive versions was also dealt with in the case of Manja v Government of the Republic of Namibia, and the court held that 

	‘[35] In National Employers’ General Insurance v Jagers, Eksteen AJP discussed the approach to mutually destructive evidence and stated the following: ‘In a civil case … where the onus rests on the plaintiff as in the present case, and where there are two mutually destructive stories, he can only succeed if he satisfies the Court on a preponderance of probabilities that his version is true and accurate and therefore acceptable, and that the other version advanced by the defendant is therefore false or mistaken and falls to be rejected.’

[32]	The court in the matter of Namdeb (Pty) Ltd v Gaseb remarked the following regarding failure to challenge the version of the opposing witness: 
	
	‘It is trite law that a party who calls a witness is entitled to assume that such a witness’s evidence has been accepted as correct if it has not been challenged in cross-examination. In Small v Smith 1954 (3) SA 434 (S.W.A) at 438E-G the following was said in respect of this aspect: “It is, in my opinion, elementary and standard practice for a party to put to each opposing witness so much of his own case or defence as concerns that witness and if need be to inform him, if he has not been given notice thereof, that other witnesses will contradict him, so as to give him fair warning and an opportunity of explaining the contradiction and defending his own character. It is grossly unfair and improper to let a witness’s evidence go unchallenged in crossexamination and afterwards argue that he must be disbelieved. Once a witness’s evidence on a point in dispute has been deliberately left unchallenged in cross-examination and particularly by a legal practitioner, the party calling that witness is normally entitled to assume in the absence of a notice to the contrary that the witness’s testimony is accepted as correct. . . . unless the testimony is so manifestly absurd, fantastic or of so romancing a character that no reasonable person can attach any credence to it whatsoever.” ’

[33]	In the case of Kolela v Minister of Home Affairs, Safety and Security, the facts of which are similar to the case before court, the plaintiff was assaulted by correctional officers and sought damages in the amount of N$50 000. The court stated that in cases of assault, the plaintiff bears the onus to prove that there was a violation of his or her bodily integrity by the defendants and that violation, if proved, is prima facie unlawful. Once the infringement is proved, the onus shifts to the defendant, to show some legal justification.

Discussion and findings

[34]	The court is tasked to determine which version presented to court is more believable. In the case of Stellenbosch Farmers Winery Group Ltd and Another v Martell et Cie and Others the court held that, to come to a conclusion on the disputed issues, a court must consider and make findings on (a) the credibility of the various factual witnesses, (b) their reliability, and (c) the probabilities.  In the current matter both parties presented multiple witnesses and when the court evaluates their credibility, the court must find that the credibility of all the witnesses cannot be faulted.  During cross examination of these witnesses, no glaring credibility issues were pointed out.  Regarding the reliability of the witnesses the versions presented on behalf of the plaintiff and the evidence presented on behalf of the defendants, the court finds that generally the witnesses were all reliable.  However when the probabilities of the evidence presented is reviewed, the court finds that the evidence presented by the defendant is in the opinion of the court, more probable.  In making this finding, the court is also sensitive that it will impact on the reliability and credibility findings made earlier.

[35]	The court further accepts that there was some form of assault on the body of the plaintiff but that assault was limited to necessary force as authorized in terms of Regulation 194 of the Namibian Correctional Service Regulations.  From the evidence presented on behalf of the defendants it seems that the plaintiff became aggressive whilst the officers were conducting a search which was also authorized by the Correctional Service Act, 9 of 2012 and the above mentioned regulations.  Based on the evidence presented by Josef Moses it is further found that the type of fracture that the tooth of the plaintiff suffered is one not related to an assault as it was an inner tooth fracture.  The evidence further shows that the plaintiff complained about his teeth on previous occasions.  The J88 further recorded no additional injuries except for a red spot in his eye and a complaint about a sensitive wrist.  There was no evidence specifically lead regarding how the eye came to have a red spot, including medical evidence to explain the type and possible cause of such a spot.  The court thus concludes that the tender wrist of the plaintiff was most probably caused by being handcuffed, and that such handcuffing occurred when the plaintiff was restrained. 	

[36]	The plaintiff also testified that he only spent about N$5000 for the replacement of his tooth, and thus, the defendants submit that damages of N$500,000 for medical expenses is exorbitant. He also failed to call the medical doctors who attended to him to corroborate his evidence. Furthermore, the plaintiff was unable to quantify the amount he claims for countemelia and trauma as per his particulars of claim. His claim for countemelia is unsubstantiated and thus should not be entertained by this Honourable Court. 

[37]	In the result, I make the following order:

1.	The claim of the plaintiff is dismissed with costs.

Arguments by the parties

[24]	The Plaintiff’s version before the court was that he was assaulted by the correctional officers, slapped by the third Defendant (witness number 4), kicked with booted feet, and stomped on his head and in the process broke his tooth. Plaintiff further testified he was bleeding and his mouth was swollen, his version was corroborated by the three witnesses who came across as credible witnesses. The Defendant’s evidence is that the officers never assaulted the Plaintiff, they testified that minimum force as provided for by the Correctional Service Act and its Regulations was used to restrain and handcuff the Plaintiff as he was aggressive. All witnesses failed to put on record how the Plaintiff was aggressive. The Defendant’s further evidence was that the Plaintiff was restrained by approximately 8 officers. It was also the Defendant’s evidence that the Plaintiff was taken to the facility clinic after complaining of pain. The court is faced with two mutually destructive versions.

[25]	It was submitted that the explanation by the plaintiff that he broke this tooth that day, and he was bleeding and swollen, is the most probable version before the court. This version was corroborated by three witnesses, and the evidence that the plaintiff was bleeding and swollen was never refuted or challenged by the defendants legal practitioner during cross-examination. The evidence adduced by the plaintiff and his witnesses regarding the bleeding was left unchallenged in cross-examination.

[26]	It was further argued that the plaintiff testified that he was handcuffed and attacked by approximately 10 officers. This version was confirmed by the defendants witnesses that about 8 officers who were present. The defendants case was that they needed to use so many officers, because the plaintiff was aggressive; however, when put to the witnesses how aggressive the plaintiff was, they failed to demonstrate to the court. Witness Ipinge Sakaria was very evasive when the question of aggression was put to him, and as such, his evidence must be approached with caution. The only reasonable inference that can be drawn is that in this scuffle, comparing the ratio of the officers to the offender, the plaintiff lost his tooth in the process. The version that reflects what truly transpired on 2 May 2022 is that of the plaintiff.

[27]	It was argued on behalf of the defendants that it is a fact that in cases of assault, the plaintiff bears the onus to prove that there was a violation of his body by the defendants and that violation, if proved, I wrongful and unlawful. Once that is proved, the onus shifts to the defendants to find some sort of legal justification, such as self-defence.  In the current instance, this was not done and the only evidence before court suggests that the third defendant and fellow officers only used minimum force, as allowed for by legislation and regulations, to restrain the plaintiff and to subsequently cuff him.  There is no evidence that he was kicked with booted feet all over his body and head.

[28]	The plaintiff, during his evidence did not focus on any emotional and psychological shock, his claim is thus not substantiated. Rather, the plaintiff focused on the alleged assault and past and future medical expenses.

The legal considerations

[29]	In Harold Schmidt t/a Prestige Home Innovations v Heita it was held that: 

	‘The correct approach would be for the court to apply its mind not only to the merits and demerits of the two mutually destructive versions but also their probabilities and it is only after so applying its mind that the court would be justified in reaching the conclusion as to which opinion to accept and which to reject’

[30]	The court in the case of Von Wielligh v Shaumbwako adopted the reasoning when faced with disparate versions, as follows: 

	‘The plaintiff can only succeed if he satisfies the court on a preponderance of probabilities that his version is true and accurate and therefore acceptable, and that the other version advanced by the defendant is therefore false or mistaken and falls to be rejected. In deciding whether that evidence is true or not the Court will weigh up and test the plaintiff’s allegations against the general probabilities. The estimate of the credibility of a witness will therefore be inextricably bound up with the consideration of the probabilities of the case and, if the balance of probabilities favour the plaintiff then the Court will accept his version as being probably true.’

[31]	The principle of mutually destructive versions was also dealt with in the case of Manja v Government of the Republic of Namibia, and the court held that 

	‘[35] In National Employers’ General Insurance v Jagers, Eksteen AJP discussed the approach to mutually destructive evidence and stated the following: ‘In a civil case … where the onus rests on the plaintiff as in the present case, and where there are two mutually destructive stories, he can only succeed if he satisfies the Court on a preponderance of probabilities that his version is true and accurate and therefore acceptable, and that the other version advanced by the defendant is therefore false or mistaken and falls to be rejected.’

[32]	The court in the matter of Namdeb (Pty) Ltd v Gaseb remarked the following regarding failure to challenge the version of the opposing witness: 
	
	‘It is trite law that a party who calls a witness is entitled to assume that such a witness’s evidence has been accepted as correct if it has not been challenged in cross-examination. In Small v Smith 1954 (3) SA 434 (S.W.A) at 438E-G the following was said in respect of this aspect: “It is, in my opinion, elementary and standard practice for a party to put to each opposing witness so much of his own case or defence as concerns that witness and if need be to inform him, if he has not been given notice thereof, that other witnesses will contradict him, so as to give him fair warning and an opportunity of explaining the contradiction and defending his own character. It is grossly unfair and improper to let a witness’s evidence go unchallenged in crossexamination and afterwards argue that he must be disbelieved. Once a witness’s evidence on a point in dispute has been deliberately left unchallenged in cross-examination and particularly by a legal practitioner, the party calling that witness is normally entitled to assume in the absence of a notice to the contrary that the witness’s testimony is accepted as correct. . . . unless the testimony is so manifestly absurd, fantastic or of so romancing a character that no reasonable person can attach any credence to it whatsoever.” ’

[33]	In the case of Kolela v Minister of Home Affairs, Safety and Security, the facts of which are similar to the case before court, the plaintiff was assaulted by correctional officers and sought damages in the amount of N$50 000. The court stated that in cases of assault, the plaintiff bears the onus to prove that there was a violation of his or her bodily integrity by the defendants and that violation, if proved, is prima facie unlawful. Once the infringement is proved, the onus shifts to the defendant, to show some legal justification.

Discussion and findings

[34]	The court is tasked to determine which version presented to court is more believable. In the case of Stellenbosch Farmers Winery Group Ltd and Another v Martell et Cie and Others the court held that, to come to a conclusion on the disputed issues, a court must consider and make findings on (a) the credibility of the various factual witnesses, (b) their reliability, and (c) the probabilities.  In the current matter both parties presented multiple witnesses and when the court evaluates their credibility, the court must find that the credibility of all the witnesses cannot be faulted.  During cross examination of these witnesses, no glaring credibility issues were pointed out.  Regarding the reliability of the witnesses the versions presented on behalf of the plaintiff and the evidence presented on behalf of the defendants, the court finds that generally the witnesses were all reliable.  However when the probabilities of the evidence presented is reviewed, the court finds that the evidence presented by the defendant is in the opinion of the court, more probable.  In making this finding, the court is also sensitive that it will impact on the reliability and credibility findings made earlier.

[35]	The court further accepts that there was some form of assault on the body of the plaintiff but that assault was limited to necessary force as authorized in terms of Regulation 194 of the Namibian Correctional Service Regulations.  From the evidence presented on behalf of the defendants it seems that the plaintiff became aggressive whilst the officers were conducting a search which was also authorized by the Correctional Service Act, 9 of 2012 and the above mentioned regulations.  Based on the evidence presented by Josef Moses it is further found that the type of fracture that the tooth of the plaintiff suffered is one not related to an assault as it was an inner tooth fracture.  The evidence further shows that the plaintiff complained about his teeth on previous occasions.  The J88 further recorded no additional injuries except for a red spot in his eye and a complaint about a sensitive wrist.  There was no evidence specifically lead regarding how the eye came to have a red spot, including medical evidence to explain the type and possible cause of such a spot.  The court thus concludes that the tender wrist of the plaintiff was most probably caused by being handcuffed, and that such handcuffing occurred when the plaintiff was restrained. 	

[36]	The plaintiff also testified that he only spent about N$5000 for the replacement of his tooth, and thus, the defendants submit that damages of N$500,000 for medical expenses is exorbitant. He also failed to call the medical doctors who attended to him to corroborate his evidence. Furthermore, the plaintiff was unable to quantify the amount he claims for countemelia and trauma as per his particulars of claim. His claim for countemelia is unsubstantiated and thus should not be entertained by this Honourable Court. 

[37]	In the result, I make the following order:

1.	The claim of the plaintiff is dismissed with costs.

The version that reflects what truly transpired on 2 May 2022 is that of the plaintiff.

[27]	It was argued on behalf of the defendants that it is a fact that in cases of assault, the plaintiff bears the onus to prove that there was a violation of his body by the defendants and that violation, if proved, I wrongful and unlawful. Once that is proved, the onus shifts to the defendants to find some sort of legal justification, such as self-defence.  In the current instance, this was not done and the only evidence before court suggests that the third defendant and fellow officers only used minimum force, as allowed for by legislation and regulations, to restrain the plaintiff and to subsequently cuff him.  There is no evidence that he was kicked with booted feet all over his body and head.

[28]	The plaintiff, during his evidence did not focus on any emotional and psychological shock, his claim is thus not substantiated. Rather, the plaintiff focused on the alleged assault and past and future medical expenses.

The legal considerations

[29]	In Harold Schmidt t/a Prestige Home Innovations v Heita it was held that: 

	‘The correct approach would be for the court to apply its mind not only to the merits and demerits of the two mutually destructive versions but also their probabilities and it is only after so applying its mind that the court would be justified in reaching the conclusion as to which opinion to accept and which to reject’

[30]	The court in the case of Von Wielligh v Shaumbwako adopted the reasoning when faced with disparate versions, as follows: 

	‘The plaintiff can only succeed if he satisfies the court on a preponderance of probabilities that his version is true and accurate and therefore acceptable, and that the other version advanced by the defendant is therefore false or mistaken and falls to be rejected. In deciding whether that evidence is true or not the Court will weigh up and test the plaintiff’s allegations against the general probabilities. The estimate of the credibility of a witness will therefore be inextricably bound up with the consideration of the probabilities of the case and, if the balance of probabilities favour the plaintiff then the Court will accept his version as being probably true.’

[31]	The principle of mutually destructive versions was also dealt with in the case of Manja v Government of the Republic of Namibia, and the court held that 

	‘[35] In National Employers’ General Insurance v Jagers, Eksteen AJP discussed the approach to mutually destructive evidence and stated the following: ‘In a civil case … where the onus rests on the plaintiff as in the present case, and where there are two mutually destructive stories, he can only succeed if he satisfies the Court on a preponderance of probabilities that his version is true and accurate and therefore acceptable, and that the other version advanced by the defendant is therefore false or mistaken and falls to be rejected.’

[32]	The court in the matter of Namdeb (Pty) Ltd v Gaseb remarked the following regarding failure to challenge the version of the opposing witness: 
	
	‘It is trite law that a party who calls a witness is entitled to assume that such a witness’s evidence has been accepted as correct if it has not been challenged in cross-examination. In Small v Smith 1954 (3) SA 434 (S.W.A) at 438E-G the following was said in respect of this aspect: “It is, in my opinion, elementary and standard practice for a party to put to each opposing witness so much of his own case or defence as concerns that witness and if need be to inform him, if he has not been given notice thereof, that other witnesses will contradict him, so as to give him fair warning and an opportunity of explaining the contradiction and defending his own character. It is grossly unfair and improper to let a witness’s evidence go unchallenged in crossexamination and afterwards argue that he must be disbelieved. Once a witness’s evidence on a point in dispute has been deliberately left unchallenged in cross-examination and particularly by a legal practitioner, the party calling that witness is normally entitled to assume in the absence of a notice to the contrary that the witness’s testimony is accepted as correct. . . . unless the testimony is so manifestly absurd, fantastic or of so romancing a character that no reasonable person can attach any credence to it whatsoever.” ’

[33]	In the case of Kolela v Minister of Home Affairs, Safety and Security, the facts of which are similar to the case before court, the plaintiff was assaulted by correctional officers and sought damages in the amount of N$50 000. The court stated that in cases of assault, the plaintiff bears the onus to prove that there was a violation of his or her bodily integrity by the defendants and that violation, if proved, is prima facie unlawful. Once the infringement is proved, the onus shifts to the defendant, to show some legal justification.

Discussion and findings

[34]	The court is tasked to determine which version presented to court is more believable. In the case of Stellenbosch Farmers Winery Group Ltd and Another v Martell et Cie and Others the court held that, to come to a conclusion on the disputed issues, a court must consider and make findings on (a) the credibility of the various factual witnesses, (b) their reliability, and (c) the probabilities.  In the current matter both parties presented multiple witnesses and when the court evaluates their credibility, the court must find that the credibility of all the witnesses cannot be faulted.  During cross examination of these witnesses, no glaring credibility issues were pointed out.  Regarding the reliability of the witnesses the versions presented on behalf of the plaintiff and the evidence presented on behalf of the defendants, the court finds that generally the witnesses were all reliable.  However when the probabilities of the evidence presented is reviewed, the court finds that the evidence presented by the defendant is in the opinion of the court, more probable.  In making this finding, the court is also sensitive that it will impact on the reliability and credibility findings made earlier.

[35]	The court further accepts that there was some form of assault on the body of the plaintiff but that assault was limited to necessary force as authorized in terms of Regulation 194 of the Namibian Correctional Service Regulations.  From the evidence presented on behalf of the defendants it seems that the plaintiff became aggressive whilst the officers were conducting a search which was also authorized by the Correctional Service Act, 9 of 2012 and the above mentioned regulations.  Based on the evidence presented by Josef Moses it is further found that the type of fracture that the tooth of the plaintiff suffered is one not related to an assault as it was an inner tooth fracture.  The evidence further shows that the plaintiff complained about his teeth on previous occasions.  The J88 further recorded no additional injuries except for a red spot in his eye and a complaint about a sensitive wrist.  There was no evidence specifically lead regarding how the eye came to have a red spot, including medical evidence to explain the type and possible cause of such a spot.  The court thus concludes that the tender wrist of the plaintiff was most probably caused by being handcuffed, and that such handcuffing occurred when the plaintiff was restrained. 	

[36]	The plaintiff also testified that he only spent about N$5000 for the replacement of his tooth, and thus, the defendants submit that damages of N$500,000 for medical expenses is exorbitant. He also failed to call the medical doctors who attended to him to corroborate his evidence. Furthermore, the plaintiff was unable to quantify the amount he claims for countemelia and trauma as per his particulars of claim. His claim for countemelia is unsubstantiated and thus should not be entertained by this Honourable Court. 

[37]	In the result, I make the following order:

1.	The claim of the plaintiff is dismissed with costs.
